question: What is the main job of the accessory organs in our digestive system?

options.A: To provide chemical secretions like enzymes and bile
options.B: To absorb all water from digested food materials
options.C: To physically push food forward using strong muscles
options.D: To serve as the primary storage tube for waste

explanation: Think of accessory organs as your digestive helpers! Instead of holding food inside a tube like the stomach or intestines, they pump in helpful chemical juices—like enzymes and bile—to break down your food. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT an accessory organ of digestion?
explanation: Food actually passes right through the stomach as part of the main tube (alimentary canal). The liver, pancreas, and gallbladder sit off to the side as trusty helpers, making them accessory organs! [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h1)

question: What is the main job of salivary amylase in your mouth?

options.A: Breaking down complex starches into simpler sugars
options.B: Dissolving dietary proteins into basic amino acids
options.C: Destroying harmful bacteria found in drinking water
options.D: Lubricating the esophagus to prevent tearing

explanation: Salivary amylase starts working the moment you chew! It targets starchy foods (like rice or yam) right in your mouth, turning them into simpler sugars before they even reach your stomach. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h2)

question: A patient with damaged salivary glands will most likely struggle with which early step of digestion?

options.A: Absorbing water from the digested food bolus
options.B: Producing insulin to control blood sugar levels
options.C: Releasing bile acids to break down dietary fats
options.D: Forming a moist bolus for easy swallowing

explanation: Without enough saliva, food stays dry and scratchy, making it really tough (and uncomfortable!) to form a smooth ball (bolus) and swallow safely. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h2)

question: Which blood vessel brings nutrient-rich blood straight from the intestines to the liver?
explanation: The hepatic portal vein is like a dedicated highway taking all the good nutrients you just absorbed from your food straight to the liver for filtering and processing first! [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h3)

question: Why is the liver considered such a vital metabolic organ for the whole body?

options.A: It processes nutrients, filters toxins, and stores essential vitamins
options.B: It produces strong mechanical churning motions to break down fiber
options.C: It pumps oxygenated blood directly through the major heart valves
options.D: It absorbs all water from solid waste before elimination

explanation: The liver is like the body's ultimate multitasking chemical factory. It handles nutrients, cleans out toxins, and stores vitamins to keep everything running smoothly. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is the main job of bile salts during fat digestion?

options.A: Neutralizing stomach acid in the duodenum
options.B: Emulsifying large fat droplets into smaller ones
options.C: Digesting complex starches into simple sugars
options.D: Killing harmful bacteria found in raw foods

explanation: Bile salts act like dish soap on greasy plates! They break big fat drops into tiny little droplets so your digestive enzymes can easily mix in and finish the job. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h4)

question: What happens to bile between meals when your body doesn't need it right away?

options.A: It is filtered out by the kidneys and eliminated in urine
options.B: It is broken down into simple sugars by liver enzymes
options.C: It is stored and concentrated inside the gallbladder
options.D: It is sent back to the stomach to digest proteins

explanation: When you're not eating, your gallbladder acts like a storage pouch, holding onto bile and thickening it up until you eat something fatty and it's time to squeeze it out. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why does the pancreas release bicarbonate ions into the small intestine?

options.A: To stimulate the gallbladder to release stored bile
options.B: To neutralize acidic chyme coming from the stomach
options.C: To break down complex proteins into amino acids
options.D: To lower blood sugar levels after a heavy meal

explanation: Food coming from the stomach is super acidic. The pancreas sends out bicarbonate (think of it like natural baking soda) to calm down that acid so it doesn't burn your intestines! [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h5)

question: How does the pancreas manage to do both exocrine and endocrine jobs?

options.A: It produces bile in the liver and stores it inside the gallbladder
options.B: It secretes digestive enzymes into ducts and hormones directly into blood
options.C: It chews food in the mouth and absorbs nutrients in the large intestine
options.D: It filters toxins from the blood and releases waste through the urine

explanation: The pancreas wears two hats! Through tiny tubes (ducts), it sends out digestive juices (exocrine), and straight into the bloodstream, it sends out hormones like insulin (endocrine). [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which hormone gets released when fats and proteins show up in the small intestine?
explanation: Cholecystokinin (let's just call it CCK!) is the hormone that shouts to the gallbladder and pancreas: 'Hey, fatty food has arrived, time to release your juices!' [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h6)

question: What triggers your small intestine to release secretin?

options.A: The complete absence of water in the bowel
options.B: The buildup of high blood sugar after a meal
options.C: The sight and smell of food before eating
options.D: The arrival of acidic chyme from the stomach

explanation: As soon as the sour, acidic food mixture leaves your stomach and hits your small intestine, secretin rushes out to call for backup (bicarbonate) to neutralize the acid. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h6)

question: What causes the yellowing of the skin and eyes that we call jaundice?

options.A: Low levels of bicarbonate in the small intestine
options.B: Rapid breakdown of red blood cells by the pancreas
options.C: A buildup of bilirubin due to blocked bile flow
options.D: An excess of salivary amylase in the bloodstream

explanation: When bile channels get blocked (maybe by a gallstone or liver trouble), a yellow pigment called bilirubin can't escape properly. It builds up in the body and turns the skin and eyes yellow. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h7)

question: A patient with severe liver cirrhosis is most likely to develop which complication due to backed-up portal blood flow?

options.A: High levels of pancreatic enzymes in the mouth
options.B: Ascites or fluid accumulation in the abdominal cavity
options.C: Rapid digestion of dietary fats without any bile
options.D: Excessive production of saliva causing drooling

explanation: When liver scarring (cirrhosis) makes it hard for blood to flow through properly, pressure builds up in the blood vessels. This pushes fluid out into the belly, a condition we call ascites. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T5#GNS121_U1_T5_h7)
